newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hits 4-1/2 year high vs. Japanese yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hits 4-1/2 year high vs. Japanese yen.

text.p: The dollar rose Tuesday to a four-and-a-half year high against the yen after a Japanese trade official said the weak yen was not entirely negative for Japan's economy.
The dollar also posted gains against the German mark and other European currencies.

In European trading, the dollar touched 126.52 Japanese yen, its highest level since August 1992, after the Jiji news service quoted Tsutomu Makino, Japan's Vice Trade Minister, as saying the weak yen was more positive than negative for the country's economy at the moment. The dollar later gave up some of those gains in U.S. trading but still ending solidly higher.
The dollar has risen strongly since U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Friday the administration would refrain from using the dollar as an instrument of trade policy.

But Tuesday's rally lost steam in U.S. trading as investors took profits amid concerns that the dollar's rapid advance might prompt the Bank of Japan to sell dollars in the open market to slow the currency's advance.

"Of course (Makino) affected the forex market a little, but not so much I think," said Tadatoshi Taso, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi in New York. "The speed of the uptrend of the dollar is a little bit too rapid, so it's a correction of the movement."
The dollar settled at 126.30 yen in late New York trading, up from 125.58 yen on Monday.
In early overseas trading, the director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, Eisuke Sakakibara, introduced a note of caution to the market.
Sakakibara said Japanese authorities would be ready to intervene in the foreign exchange markets if rates veered sharply from economic fundamentals.

The dollar also was briefly weighed down after a Bridge News report, quoting a source close to the Clinton administration, suggested Washington was worried that Japan would rely on the weak yen to boost exports and help out a weak domestic economy and delay needed economic reforms. A weaker yen makes Japanese exports cheaper in dollar terms.
"That is sort of what I think hit the market late," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.

Elsewhere, the dollar garnered support against other key currencies from comments by Michel Camdessus, the head of the International Monetary Fund, who said the dollar was in a credible zone against European currencies and the yen.
The dollar rose to 1.7155 German marks from 1.7125 marks on Monday and to 1.4748 Swiss francs from 1.4695 Swiss.
The British pound fell to $1.6260 from $1.6278.
